annotations.text:
Fifth pass. The inputs were still too cramped in a 470px column, so they are not in a column any more.

The band runs the full width: the policy editor gets ~560px, enough that a CQL2 rule with an S_INTERSECTS polygon sits on one line instead of wrapping four times. The query chips and the principal get real room beside it.

It collapses to a one-line summary once set, so the scroll cost you pay for the width is only paid while you are editing.

The matrix is the finding now.

Zero-fill is NOT universally safe, and that is the interesting part. It is lossless exactly when the reader never parses the blanked bytes:

• DuckDB projects, so a zeroed chunk inside its 64 KiB block is never looked at — clean.
• hyparquet without projection reads all 19 columns, so it parses the zeros and hands back garbage.

Same gate, same policy, opposite outcome. That is a sharper statement than anything about range counts.

DuckDB, measured:

• projection pushdown is real — 2 of 19 columns fetched 11.9% of the object
• row-group pruning is real — a WHERE clause read 2 of 8 row groups
• and 27 of 27 content requests still straddle, because the reads are 64 KiB power-of-two blocks, not chunk extents

Deny `extra`, ask for `fare_amount` → refused, because they are adjacent in the file. Deny `extra`, ask for `VendorID` → fine. Adjacency decides, not the query.

Open:

• The collapse is the part I am least sure of. It buys full-width editing without a permanent scroll tax, but it adds a state the page can be in, and a collapsed band hides the thing a reader most needs to understand the results. Worth a look at whether it should start collapsed or expanded.

• DuckDB zero-fill "completes" is still unverified — it assumes nothing validates page headers or CRCs inside unprojected chunks.

• COG side still needs the same treatment.

• Legend moved above the charts — it was at the foot of the reader panel, which meant the first chart on the page was unreadable until you had scrolled past it.

• "Run every reader" said what it loops over, not what it does. It now reads "Run this query / three readers, same policy, every range checked" — the subject is the query you built in step 1, executed three times against the same file.
